title: Trump Says an Iran Deal Is 'Largely Negotiated.' India Is Watching the Strait.
excerpt: A proposed 60-day ceasefire extension and reopening of the Strait of Hormuz would ease the energy shock that has battered India's economy for three months. But the nuclear question remains unresolved.
body:
President Donald Trump declared on Saturday that a peace agreement with Iran has been "largely negotiated," announcing what could be the most significant diplomatic breakthrough since the United States and Israel launched their war against Tehran on February 28.

The announcement, made on Truth Social following conference calls with the leaders of Pakistan and several Gulf allies, describes a deal that would reopen the Strait of Hormuz — the maritime chokepoint through which roughly a fifth of the world's oil once transited — and extend the fragile April 8 ceasefire by 60 days.

For India, which imports over 80 per cent of its crude oil, the word "Hormuz" carries the weight of an entire economic reckoning. The strait's effective closure has driven up India's fuel import bill, contributed to a weaker rupee, and forced the Reserve Bank of India into three consecutive rate holds as inflation projections climbed to 5.1 per cent for the current fiscal year. A reopening, even a partial one, would begin to relieve the pressure that has defined India's macroeconomic reality since March.

## The Deal on the Table

According to NBC News, negotiators from both sides have reached broad agreement, though final sign-off from Trump and Iran's supreme leader remains pending. Vice President JD Vance confirmed progress but noted sticking points. "We're going back and forth on a couple of language points," Vance said. "I do think we've made a lot of progress here."

The proposed framework would see Iran reopen the Strait of Hormuz immediately, followed by a 60-day negotiating window focused on Tehran's nuclear programme and its enriched uranium stockpiles — most of which were destroyed by US strikes during the initial weeks of the war.

Iran's Foreign Ministry indicated that nuclear limitations could be deferred to the extended negotiations. Tehran wants access to billions of dollars in frozen oil revenue, relief from sanctions on crude exports, and the lifting of the US naval blockade imposed on its ports since April 13.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio was direct about American conditions: "Open the Strait, highly enriched uranium, no nuclear programme." Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent echoed the line, saying sanctions relief would not be considered until those conditions are met.

## A Ceasefire That Never Fully Held

Saturday's diplomatic optimism came against the backdrop of continued violence. Just hours before Trump's announcement, US Central Command reported shooting down four Iranian drones targeting maritime traffic near the Strait and striking Iranian coastal radar sites at Goruk and Qeshm Island.

Iran's Revolutionary Guards retaliated by firing seven ballistic missiles at US bases in Kuwait and Bahrain. Six were intercepted; the seventh fell short. Kuwait reported material damage but no casualties.

The pattern has repeated throughout the ceasefire period. This week alone saw Iran launch 30 missiles and drones at Kuwait, damaging the country's international airport, killing one person and injuring dozens. Each exchange has been described by both sides as "defensive," a diplomatic fiction that grows thinner with every salvo.

## What It Means for the Indian Diaspora

The war's impact on the Indian diaspora extends well beyond fuel prices. An estimated 8.5 million Indians live and work across the Gulf states — in the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, and Oman. The repeated missile attacks on Kuwait, where hundreds of thousands of Indian workers are based, have rattled families across India and forced the Indian embassy in Kuwait City into near-continuous crisis mode. An Indian worker was killed in a recent strike on Kuwait's airport.

Remittances from the Gulf account for a significant share of India's foreign exchange inflows. Prolonged instability threatens not just physical safety but the economic lifeline that connects millions of Indian families to their relatives abroad.

## Pakistan's Mediating Role

Behind the diplomatic language sits an unlikely mediator: Pakistan. Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi arrived in Tehran on Saturday for talks with Iranian officials, including Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi. A Pakistani source confirmed that Naqvi carried a message intended for Iran's supreme leader, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei.

Pakistan's central role has drawn scrutiny. Israel's Consul General in Mumbai, Yaniv Revach, said the arrangement was "not ideal" but acknowledged that it had brought the sides closer. "Both sides are working through final adjustments, and clarity on the agreement's implementation is anticipated soon," he said.

India, for its part, has maintained what diplomats call "strategic ambiguity" — engaging both Washington and Tehran while advocating de-escalation. Prime Minister Modi's five-nation European and Gulf tour last week was widely interpreted as an effort to diversify energy partnerships and build resilience against exactly this kind of disruption.

## The Road Ahead

The deal, if finalised, would not end the conflict. Nuclear negotiations would continue for two months. Israel's Prime Minister Netanyahu, who had hoped the joint military campaign would lead to regime change in Tehran, faces disappointment. But Trump reportedly spoke with Netanyahu on Saturday and described the call as having "gone very well."

On Capitol Hill, bipartisan support for any deal that lowers fuel prices is strong. "The farmers here in Kentucky can't afford the fertilizer to put on their fields, so heck yes, I would support it," said Representative Thomas Massie.

For India, even a temporary reopening of the Strait would ease the immediate pain. But the structural vulnerability the crisis exposed — an 80 per cent dependence on imported crude, concentrated shipping routes, and a currency hostage to global oil prices — will not disappear with a ceasefire. The lesson of the last three months is clear: energy diversification is no longer a policy aspiration. It is a survival imperative.
